inserts.title: Fink–Heimer staining marks downstream terminals
paragraphs: Fink–Heimer staining reveals degenerating fibers and terminals after a neuron is damaged. Because the stain marks only processes that lost their cell body, it shows which axons a lesioned population sends out. Nottebohm and colleagues applied this stain to canary song nuclei, so the lesion sites map onto a visible pathway of degenerating fibers.

After lesions of the region historically called HVc, degenerating fibers were found in RA. Degeneration in RA then pointed toward descending pathways that reach vocal motor structures in the brainstem. Each labeled tract starts at a known lesion and ends at a known target.

The anatomy therefore supplies a direction for the song pathway, independent of any change in the song itself. A lesion that disrupts song and a lesion that produces degeneration in RA point to the same chain of nuclei, which makes the pathway easier to trace. Each stained tract can be followed back to a lesioned population.

inserts.title: Single-cell filling reveals complete local arbors
paragraphs: **Single-cell filling** labels one neuron completely so that its dendrites and axons can be traced in full. Benezra and colleagues filled identified HVC neurons after labeling them through their output targets. A filled cell therefore carries both its anatomy and the target that defines it.

Two-photon imaging resolved the fine branches of these cells inside living tissue. The reconstructions were then built from serial sections, so each arbor could be followed across the boundaries of the slices. The complete branching pattern is visible only when a single cell is isolated from its neighbors.

Each filled neuron keeps its own branching pattern, so a reconstruction shows one cell's arbor rather than an average of many cells. Its dendrites and axonal branches show how far that neuron's signals can travel within HVC. The arbor is the anatomical basis for its local influence, and projection identity links the filled cell to its output target.

inserts.title: Local axons vary within the RA-projecting population
paragraphs: A **local axon collateral** is a branch that stays within the same nucleus as its parent cell. Benezra and colleagues measured these branches in HVC(RA) neurons, which send their long axons to RA. The branches show how much each cell contacts the tissue around it.

Some HVC(RA) neurons kept most of their local branches close to the cell body. Others spread their branches across a larger part of HVC, so two cells with the same long-range target can influence different amounts of local tissue. Cells that share one output target therefore differ in their local arbor, which sets their local influence.

Local branches therefore give each RA-projecting cell its own position in the HVC network. A neuron with broad local branches can influence more of the surrounding tissue before its signal reaches RA. The branching pattern of each cell is therefore recorded as an individual property.

inserts.title: Temperature sets the width and rate of RA spikes
paragraphs: **Spike half-width** is the duration of an action potential measured at half its peak height. Zemel and colleagues measured this value in identified RA projection neurons at about 40 °C, close to the body temperature of the bird. The spikes were very brief, with a half-width near 0.18 ms. The temperature of the recording is part of the measurement, so the value applies to warm slices.

Spontaneous spikes at about 40 °C fired roughly four times faster than at room temperature. Depolarizing current evoked sustained trains of rapid spikes, which shows that these neurons sustain fast firing when driven. The width and rate of the spike are both set by the recording temperature, which is part of the spike's physiology.

Temperature therefore changes the speed of the motor neuron's output. Spike width and firing rate both depend on conditions, so the same cell can have a different timing profile in a warm slice and in a cool one. Each recording therefore reflects the temperature at which it was made.

inserts.title: Resurgent current rises with age in males
paragraphs: A resurgent sodium current is a current that reappears as the membrane repolarizes after a strong depolarization. Zemel and colleagues measured it alongside the transient sodium current in the same RA neurons. Measuring both currents within one sweep isolates the resurgent component from the overall sodium current, so the developmental record of this component is taken from the same cells.

The recordings covered birds at 20, 35 and 50 days after hatching and adult males. Resurgent current increased with age, including after normalization to the transient current. The result shows that the increase is specific to the resurgent component rather than a general rise in all sodium current.

The developmental change therefore follows the maturation of the neuron's sodium channels. Because the current grows over the same period as song development, it is a candidate contributor to the faster firing of mature motor neurons. The developmental result is therefore a measurement of the current itself.

inserts.title: Dynamic clamp moves resurgent current into real neurons
paragraphs: **Dynamic clamp** is a recording method that calculates a current from the membrane voltage in real time and injects it into a neuron. Zemel and colleagues used it to add a resurgent-current component to juvenile RA neurons. The same method subtracted a corresponding component from adult neurons.

Adding the component increased the firing frequency of juvenile neurons. Subtracting it reduced the firing of adult neurons. Because the same cell was tested with the intervention off and on, the immediate effect of the current could be separated from differences between cells of different ages.

This manipulation tests whether resurgent current contributes to firing, rather than only correlating with it. The injected conductance was calibrated against the measured sodium-current kinetics, so the added current matches the one recorded in the cells. Each manipulation is tested on the same cell before and after the intervention.

inserts.title: Apamin changes spike timing without changing mean rate
paragraphs: **Apamin** is a toxin that blocks SK channels, which are calcium-activated potassium channels. Hou and colleagues applied it to RA projection neurons and recorded their spontaneous spikes before and after the drug. The same cells were compared in both conditions.

The interval between successive spikes became more variable after apamin. The average firing rate changed little, so the regularity of the spike train changed independently of its speed. A neuron can therefore fire at the same rate with more or less reproducible timing.

SK channels shape the return toward threshold after each action potential. Blocking them makes the spike train less regular, which means that timing precision is a property separate from firing rate. Each neuron's spike train is recorded before and after the drug, so the change in regularity is measured within the same cell.

inserts.title: Dopamine raises RA neuronal firing reversibly
paragraphs: **Dopamine** is a neuromodulator that changes the excitability of neurons through receptor signaling. Liao and colleagues applied dopamine to adult RA projection neurons while controlling the injected current. The same cell was recorded before, during and after the drug.

Firing rose during the dopamine application and returned toward baseline after the wash. The membrane potential also shifted toward a less negative value. The reversal within each cell shows that the effect came from the drug rather than from a difference between neurons.

The depolarization makes RA neurons closer to firing for the same input. This change in excitability is a candidate mechanism for how dopamine alters the output of the motor nucleus during song-related activity. The effect is therefore a property of the cells in this preparation.

inserts.title: D1-like and D2-like agonists act differently on RA
paragraphs: A **D1-like receptor** and a **D2-like receptor** are two classes of dopamine receptor that act through different signaling pathways. Liao and colleagues compared the effect of a D1-like agonist with that of a D2-like agonist on RA neurons. The two drugs were tested on the same kind of cell. Each agonist was tested under the same recording conditions.

The D2-like agonist quinpirole did not reproduce the strong increase in excitability produced by dopamine. The D1-like agonist did produce a comparable increase. The two agonists therefore produced different effects in the same preparation.

The receptor class determines whether dopamine excites RA neurons. The result constrains how dopamine acts on the motor nucleus, because a single transmitter can produce different responses through different receptors. The receptor comparison uses the D1-like result as its reference.

inserts.title: Stronger HVC synapses increase during development
paragraphs: A **single-fiber response** is a current evoked by activating one input fiber at a time. Garst-Orozco and colleagues used weak stimulation to isolate these responses on RA neurons. Stronger stimulation was used to recruit the full population of inputs, so the two measures can be compared.

Median single-fiber HVC currents rose from about 23 pA in subsong birds to about 60 pA in adults. The estimated number of recruited inputs first increased and then declined. The synapses therefore grew stronger while the number of active inputs was refined.

This pattern describes refinement rather than a uniform increase in every aspect of connectivity. The strengthening of individual HVC inputs can change how RA converts HVC activity into motor output over the course of development. Each measurement is kept separate so that connection strength is not confused with input number.

inserts.title: Stage comparisons separate intrinsic and synaptic change
paragraphs: **Input-to-firing gain** is the change in output firing for a given increase in input current. Garst-Orozco and colleagues measured this gain in RA neurons across subsong, plastic-song and adult stages. The gain and spike-frequency adaptation were broadly similar across these groups.

Zemel and colleagues instead tested younger 20-day birds and isolated sodium-current components. They reported a pronounced maturation of resurgent current and spike properties over the same developmental period. The two studies used different ages and different measurements, so their results address different questions.

A stable firing-rate response over one age interval fits with an earlier maturation of a particular ion current. The two results together show that RA intrinsic properties change in some respects and stay stable in others. The developmental account therefore depends on which property is measured at which age.

inserts.title: Tracers show LMAN output to Area X and RA
paragraphs: A **retrograde tracer** labels neurons that project toward an injection site, whereas an **anterograde tracer** labels the axons and terminals that leave a site. Vates and Nottebohm used both kinds of tracer to map connections between song nuclei. The two directions together show which cells send a projection and where it ends.

Injections associated with Area X and RA labeled neurons and terminal fields in LMAN. These findings supported an output route from LMAN to both the basal ganglia region and the motor nucleus. The circuit therefore extends beyond the one-way chain from HVC to the vocal organ.

Projections in both directions make the song circuit more interconnected than a single chain. A forebrain nucleus can send information to the motor pathway as well as to the basal ganglia, which shapes how the song system can be studied as a network.

inserts.title: Playback trials compare self-song with control sounds
paragraphs: A **playback** experiment presents a recorded sound to an animal while its neural responses are recorded. Doupe played the bird's own song and comparison sounds while recording LMAN spikes in anesthetized adult zebra finches. The responses to each stimulus were compared trial by trial.

Many neurons responded strongly to the bird's own song and weakly to other conspecific songs and simple sounds. Amplitude-modulated noise and tones match the sound energy of the songs, so a generic response to loudness would show up with these controls. The response is therefore specific to the song's structure, and each neuron was tested with all of these stimuli.

The selective response therefore links an anterior forebrain nucleus to the acoustic structure of the bird's own learned song. The effect was measured under anesthesia during playback, so it describes the sensory response of the neurons rather than their behavior during singing. The selective response is a property of the neurons, not of the playback sound alone.

inserts.title: Recorded midbrain cells are identified by their labeling
paragraphs: A **juxtacellular label** is a dye delivered to a single recorded neuron after its spikes have been measured. Gale and Perkel combined this label with immunostaining for tyrosine hydroxylase, an enzyme involved in catecholamine synthesis. Marker-positive cells provide a check on the identity assigned from firing properties.

The recordings were made in the substantia nigra pars compacta and the ventral tegmental area, SNc/VTA. Cells that were classified by their spike waveform were then checked against the marker. The fluorescent micrographs carry 20 µm scale bars, so the recorded cell and its tissue can be located together.

A waveform classification gives a provisional identity, and the labeled cell confirms or revises it. The combination of recording and staining links a cell's firing pattern to its neurochemical identity, which gives a stronger identification than the waveform alone.

2: Song consists of **coordinated vocal elements**, and their frequency and timing can be measured with a **spectrogram**, which displays acoustic energy across time and frequency. Nottebohm and colleagues recorded adult male canaries before brain surgery, which established each bird's own repertoire as the behavioral baseline. Later changes were judged against that record.

The team compared postoperative vocalizations with those recordings instead of treating every change in singing as the same. Damage could reduce the number of available **syllables**, disturb their acoustic structure, or disrupt the order of phrases while leaving vocal output possible. Each of these outcomes points to a different kind of motor deficit.

A bird that still vocalizes can therefore have a severe **song-control deficit**, because the deficit lies in the organization of the song rather than in the ability to sing. These lesion experiments identified components of a learned motor behavior in adults. The learning of a tutor's song is studied separately.
3: A **lesion** is damage to tissue that tests whether a region contributes to a behavior. Nottebohm and colleagues made unilateral electrolytic lesions in adult male canaries and reconstructed each lesion's position histologically after repeated postoperative recordings. Matching every song change to its exact lesion site made the location of the effect the central variable.

Lesions involving **HVC** or the **robust nucleus of the arcopallium**, RA, severely altered song organization. Several lesions outside this pathway had little or no effect on song. Comparing effective and ineffective sites narrowed the search to a restricted set of forebrain territories.

Electrolytic current destroys the cells at a lesion and the axons that pass through it, so each lesion is reconstructed histologically and its effect is tied to the tissue it destroyed. Lesions in the restricted forebrain territories identified here are necessary for normal adult song. Matching every song change to its exact lesion site makes the location of the effect the central variable.
4: An **axon** carries signals away from a neuron, and a **projection** is an axonal connection between two regions. A **synapse** is the junction where one neuron influences another cell. Nottebohm and colleagues combined the behavioral lesions with Fink–Heimer staining, a method that reveals degenerating fibers and terminals downstream of damaged neurons.

Degeneration linked the region historically called HVc to RA, and it connected RA with descending pathways toward vocal motor structures. Comparing the lesion locations with the distribution of degeneration gave anatomical evidence that is independent of the acoustic changes in song. The two kinds of evidence therefore support the same pathway.

The original article uses historical names that differ from current avian terminology: HVC is now a proper name, and RA lies in the arcopallium. Degeneration tracing shows the anatomical direction of a pathway. Its transmitter, synaptic sign and activity during singing are measured with the methods described on the following slides.
5: A **projection neuron** sends an axon outside its local region. Benezra and colleagues distinguished HVC neurons projecting to RA, designated HVC(RA), from neurons projecting to **Area X**, a song-related basal ganglia region involved in action control. The two populations are defined by where their axons end.

They labeled individual cells in adult male zebra finches and reconstructed their dendrites and axons in three dimensions. The analysis kept the target identity of each filled neuron rather than pooling every HVC cell into one morphological class. Each reconstruction therefore carries both its anatomy and its projection target.

HVC(RA) and HVC(X) neurons differed in their dendritic and local axonal organization. Target identity did not predict every anatomical feature, so the two groups share some features while differing in others. Each population therefore receives its own description within the same set of reconstructions.
6: **Two-photon microscopy** uses nonlinear excitation to resolve fluorescent structures within tissue. Benezra and colleagues combined retrograde labeling from an HVC output target with visually guided recordings and intracellular filling. The method linked each neuron's projection identity to its later anatomical reconstruction.

A fluorescently filled neuron was processed histologically so that its dendrites and axonal branches could be traced across sections. The approach resolved single-cell structure that would be obscured if many neighboring neurons were labeled together. Each traced cell therefore stands on its own.

Targeted filling bridges an identified neuron and its complete local arbor. Incomplete filling, section boundaries and optical resolution set the detail that each reconstruction can show. The resulting anatomical map describes the cell's structure, and its functional synapses are examined by other measurements.
7: A **dendrite** is a neuronal process that receives synaptic input. Benezra and colleagues compared reconstructed dendritic trees of HVC(RA) and HVC(X) neurons after registering their positions within HVC. Registration places every cell in the same frame, so the territories of the two groups can be compared directly.

Most RA-projecting cells had relatively restricted dendritic territories, whereas X-projecting cells occupied larger territories. Displaying individual reconstructions kept the variation within each class visible. Individual reconstructions therefore remain the basis for every class average.

A broader dendritic field gives access to a different spatial distribution of potential inputs. Proximity of the dendrites to other cells is a separate matter from connectivity, and the synapses that form along the territory are measured separately.
8: Benezra and colleagues quantified dendritic length along three spatial axes and the total path length of each reconstructed HVC neuron. Centering these measurements on each cell body separated the extent of the dendrites from the neuron's absolute position within the nucleus. The two properties are therefore measured independently.

RA-projecting neurons generally formed a group with smaller dendrites, whereas X-projecting neurons formed a group with larger dendrites. The distributions included exceptions, and cells with branches to both targets did not form one uniform size class. Size therefore tracks projection target only in part.

These measurements show the spatial integration available to each projection population. Dendritic size is one feature among several, and the anatomical classes overlap in those other features even when their average organization differs. Each class is therefore described by its typical size and by the spread of individual cells around it.
9: An **axon collateral** is a branch of an axon, and a **bouton** is a swelling at a potential presynaptic terminal. Benezra and colleagues counted boutons along the reconstructed local collateral branches of HVC(RA) and HVC(X) neurons. The count measures how much local output each cell can make.

Both projection classes carried abundant boutons within HVC, with broadly similar bouton densities. The reconstruction-based estimate was about 400 local boutons per HVC(RA) neuron. The labeled micrographs keep a 5 µm scale bar that sets the size of each bouton.

Long-range projection neurons therefore also contribute to local HVC communication, in addition to sending signals downstream. Light-microscopic boutons mark candidate contact sites, and the contacts themselves are confirmed by other methods.
10: Benezra and colleagues reconstructed the dendrites and axonal collaterals of individual HVC(RA) neurons within the boundary of HVC. The descending axon identifies the cell's long-range destination, while its local branches give a separate measure of output within the nucleus. Both measures come from the same cell.

Some cells confined most of their local branches near the cell body, whereas others spread branches across a broader portion of HVC. This variation was visible within the RA-projecting population, so it is not explained only by the difference between projection targets. Individual cells differ in how far their local output reaches.

Local output makes a purely feedforward description of HVC incomplete. An RA-projecting neuron can take part in HVC interactions before its axon reaches RA. The reconstruction identifies the contact partner only as a candidate, and the cell type of each partner is tested separately.
11: **Area X** receives an HVC projection that is distinct from the direct HVC-to-RA motor pathway. Benezra and colleagues reconstructed HVC(X) neurons with their local axons, dendrites and descending projection, all identified in the same preparation.

Their local branches varied from restricted arbors to broad distributions within HVC. The authors compared these distributions with RA-projecting cells in a shared reference frame, which revealed an organization that a drawing of single cells would miss. The shared frame keeps the two populations comparable.

An HVC(X) neuron can therefore influence both the local HVC network and a distant basal ganglia region. The anatomy supports several routes by which HVC activity reaches its targets, and the timing of each route is measured separately. Comparing these cells with RA-projecting neurons shows which features each projection shares.
12: Benezra and colleagues identified HVC neurons with axonal projections toward both RA and Area X. These **HVC(RA/X)** cells challenge the idea that all long-range HVC outputs belong to two completely separate populations. Their existence changes the simple two-population picture of HVC.

The dual-projecting cells differed from one another in dendritic organization. The authors kept each one as an individually identified cell rather than forcing it into a single class defined only by its pair of targets. The individual cells therefore show more variety than the label suggests.

Dual projections offer a possible route for distributing related activity to motor and anterior forebrain pathways. The cells are rare in the reconstructions, and whether both branches carry the same information is tested by recording both targets during singing.
13: The **HVC shelf** is the tissue that borders HVC and is distinguished from the nucleus itself. Benezra and colleagues observed dendrites and axonal collaterals of an identified HVC(X) neuron extending beyond the conventional HVC boundary into this shelf.

Fluorescent and brightfield images were combined with reconstruction of the labeled processes. The original panels keep scale bars of 100 µm for the wider field and 25 µm and 5 µm for the detailed views. Those scales separate the nucleus-scale anatomy from the fine processes.

A histological boundary is therefore not always a complete boundary for a neuron's connections. These processes give anatomical access to the adjacent tissue, and the connections they make there are examined in later experiments. The processes that reach the shelf are therefore part of the anatomy that each reconstruction describes.
14: A **broadcast arbor** distributes axonal branches across a relatively broad volume, whereas a **local arbor** stays more spatially restricted. Benezra and colleagues quantified the axonal extent of each HVC neuron and the share of the nucleus that it occupied.

Both RA-projecting and X-projecting populations contained cells with different local output territories. Quantifying axonal distribution separately from dendritic distribution keeps a large input field from being treated as a large output field. The two measures stay distinct.

These anatomical differences shape how activity could spread through the HVC network. The local and broadcast categories describe reconstructed geometry, and the partners that each arbor reaches are identified in the next steps of the analysis. Each category is defined by the measured geometry of its arbor.
15: **RA** is a forebrain motor nucleus whose projection neurons send descending output to brainstem targets. Zemel and colleagues place RA within the vocal motor pathway that connects HVC with the tracheosyringeal hypoglossal nucleus, nXIIts, and the syrinx.

The **syrinx** is the avian vocal organ, and its muscles are controlled by lower motor neurons rather than directly by RA cell bodies. RA activity therefore reaches the vocal muscles through descending axons and brainstem motor connections, which coordinate the sound.

Air pressure applied around an isolated zebra finch syrinx produced sound without any input from the brain. The experiment shows that the vocal organ can generate sound on its own. Brain-driven song control therefore depends on the neural commands that shape the output of the syrinx, which the isolated preparation leaves out.
16: An **action potential** is a rapid electrical spike produced by voltage-dependent membrane conductances. An **ion channel** is a membrane protein that allows ions to cross the membrane. Zemel and colleagues recorded identified RA projection neurons in zebra finch brain slices with whole-cell current clamp, which measures membrane voltage while current is controlled.

At about 40 °C, close to the avian body temperature, spontaneous spikes had a half-width of about 0.18 ms. Spontaneous firing was about fourfold faster than at room temperature, and depolarizing current evoked sustained rapid spike trains. The narrow spikes therefore show a fast firing capacity.

Temperature changes the quantitative description of these motor neurons. Slice recordings show the intrinsic firing capacity under controlled conditions. The commands issued during a particular song syllable are recorded during singing, where patterned synaptic input and behavioral state also act on the cell.
17: A **resurgent sodium current** is an inward sodium current that appears as the membrane repolarizes after a strong depolarization. Zemel and colleagues used voltage clamp, which controls membrane voltage while recording current, to isolate this component.

A step from −90 to +30 mV activated a transient current. Subsequent test voltages evoked resurgent current, with a peak near −3 nA at −45 mV in adult RA projection neurons. The sequence of voltage steps made the later inward current measurable.

Resurgent current supports renewed excitation during recovery from a spike. The recording measures the membrane current under the imposed voltage protocol, and its contribution to firing is tested in the current-clamp experiments.
18: A sodium channel's **β subunit** is an accessory protein that changes how the channel functions. Zemel and colleagues applied in situ hybridization, which detects specific RNA sequences in tissue, to compare Navβ3 and Navβ4 expression across male zebra finch development.

The sampled stages were 20, 35 and 50 days after hatching and adulthood. RA changed from relatively strong Navβ3 expression toward stronger Navβ4 expression. Comparison with the surrounding arcopallium showed that the change is specific to RA rather than a uniform shift across nearby tissue.

RNA abundance identifies a candidate molecular mechanism. The expression data were paired with physiological recordings and with later manipulations of resurgent current, which together test whether the subunit change produces the current change.
19: Zemel and colleagues recorded transient and resurgent sodium currents from RA projection neurons at 20, 35 and 50 days after hatching and in adult male zebra finches. Applying the same voltage protocol at each stage made the current components directly comparable.

Resurgent current increased with age, including when it was normalized to the transient current measured in the same sweep. That normalization shows that the developmental effect is not simply a general increase in all sodium current. The current specifically increases relative to the transient component.

The age-related current increase tracks the shift toward Navβ4 expression, and the two changes occur together across development. The developmental pairing is then tested by changing the current directly, as the later slides describe.
20: **Space clamp** describes how well an electrode controls voltage throughout a neuron, and long axons make that control harder. Zemel and colleagues repeated the sodium-current measurements in frontal slices that shortened the initial axonal segments of RA projection neurons.

The team also lowered extracellular sodium to improve recording conditions, and they compared neurons from 20-day males with adult neurons. The developmental difference in resurgent current remained under these altered conditions. The difference therefore reflects the cells themselves rather than the recording of distant axons.

The controls leave the voltage clamp imperfect, since long axons are never fully clamped. The developmental difference in resurgent current survived shortened axons and reduced extracellular sodium, which points to a biological origin for the change. The current measured here belongs to isolated cells, and its effect on song structure is tested in the later experiments.
21: Zemel and colleagues introduced a peptide from the intracellular C-terminal region of Navβ4 through the recording pipette into RA neurons from 20-day male zebra finches. A **peptide** is a short chain of amino acids, used here to test a proposed channel mechanism.

Resurgent current increased over about 7 minutes after whole-cell access with the native peptide. A scrambled peptide containing the same amino acids in a different sequence did not produce the same increase, which controls for nonspecific effects of the peptide.

This intervention links a defined sequence to the current change more directly than RNA expression alone does. The effect is measured in isolated cells, and its consequences for the intact bird are tested in separate experiments.
22: **Dynamic clamp** computes a voltage-dependent current during the recording and injects that current into a real neuron. Zemel and colleagues used this method to add a resurgent-current component to juvenile RA neurons and to subtract a matching component from adult neurons.

Adding the component increased juvenile firing frequency, whereas subtracting it reduced adult firing. Each cell was recorded with the intervention off and then on, so the immediate effect of the current is measured within the same neuron. Stable differences between developmental groups are identified from that effect separately.

The experiment supports a causal contribution of resurgent current to neuronal excitability. The injected conductance was calibrated to the measured sodium-current kinetics, and the match with the voltage-clamp recordings ties the injected current to the current measured in the cell. Its contribution to song timing is studied in the bird itself.
23: Zemel and colleagues examined Navβ4 expression and RA physiology across ages in female zebra finches, which lack the learned courtship song that males sing. In situ hybridization was run alongside adjacent Nissl-stained sections, which places the expression pattern within the tissue. The female data cover the same ages as the male data.

Females did not show the male pattern of strong developmental Navβ4 upregulation or the mature resurgent-current specialization. The sex difference therefore reflects a developmental program specific to males. Developmental change of this kind follows the males' sex-specific program.

Male birds isolated from tutor song still developed mature firing properties. Maturation of firing therefore proceeds on the bird's own program, separate from learning a tutor's song. Imitation of a tutor's song is a different process with its own timing, and mature firing properties are the measured endpoint of the maturation program.
24: **SK channels** are small-conductance calcium-activated potassium channels. Calcium-dependent potassium efflux produces an **afterhyperpolarization**, a period of more negative membrane voltage after a spike that sets when the next spike can occur.

Hou and colleagues recorded RA projection neurons in adult male zebra finch slices and applied apamin, an SK-channel blocker, at 100 nM. In one example, the firing rate for a 100 pA stimulus rose from 34 to about 53 Hz. Blocking the channels reduced the afterhyperpolarization and increased current-evoked firing, which links the target to both the spike waveform and the excitability of the cell.

The direction of the effect fits removal of a potassium-mediated brake on excitation. The pharmacology establishes this contribution under slice conditions, and the timing of a complete song is examined with the in vivo measurements that follow.
25: **Interspike intervals** are the times that separate successive action potentials. Hou and colleagues compared spontaneous spike trains from the same RA projection neurons before and after apamin, so firing regularity could be assessed in each cell.

SK blockade increased the variability of the intervals between spikes without a clear change in the average spontaneous firing rate. The recordings therefore separate a neuron that fires faster from a neuron that fires more reproducibly.

Calcium-activated potassium feedback stabilizes the return toward spike threshold after each action potential. The result supports a contribution of SK channels to temporal regularity. The regularity of firing is therefore one property that the same cells can change without changing their mean rate.
26: A **spike threshold** is the membrane voltage at which regenerative excitation starts an action potential. Hou and colleagues evoked firing with a 100 pA depolarizing current and compared the thresholds measured before and after 100 nM apamin blocked SK channels.

Blockade increased the variation of the evoked thresholds and shifted them toward more depolarized voltages as the injected current increased. The recordings link irregular firing to less stable spike initiation, rather than assuming that every change in spike count has the same membrane cause.

The effect supports a role for calcium-activated potassium feedback in recovery between spikes. The specific calcium source that activates SK channels is identified by separate measurements, and spontaneous and current-evoked firing respond to the intervention in their own ways.
27: Hou and colleagues blocked ionotropic glutamate receptors while recording RA projection neurons. **AMPA receptors** support relatively fast excitatory transmission, whereas **NMDA receptors** have slower kinetics and voltage-dependent gating.

Apamin still increased current-evoked firing after receptor blockade. Its effect on firing regularity was no longer clearly detectable, which shows that the regularity effect depends on incoming excitation. Excitability and regularity therefore depend on different inputs to the same neuron. Glutamatergic input is blocked in these recordings, so the regularity effect is tested without it.

Intrinsic potassium conductance and incoming excitation interact to set spike timing. The control identifies the glutamatergic contribution to regularity, and the presynaptic source of that excitation is tested by separate experiments.
28: **Dopamine** is a neurotransmitter that modulates neuronal properties through receptor-dependent intracellular signaling. Liao and colleagues recorded adult male zebra finch RA projection neurons and applied 50 µM dopamine while controlling the injected current.

During a 100 pA stimulus, normalized firing rose to about 1.38 times baseline and returned toward baseline after washout. The membrane potential became less negative, shifting from about −70 to −61 mV under the reported recording conditions.

The same neuron showed reversible modulation of excitability before and after the drug, which is a direct test of the drug's effect. Bath application delivers dopamine at a different concentration and timing from physiological release. The recorded effect is therefore a property of the cell under these conditions, and behavioral state during singing is measured separately.
29: Liao and colleagues used **tetrodotoxin**, or TTX, to block voltage-gated sodium channels and prevent action potentials in the RA slice. The manipulation tests whether the dopamine-induced depolarization depended on spike-driven activity.

Dopamine still produced a depolarizing shift when sodium-dependent spikes were blocked, so the shift arises without action potentials. Spikes evoked in the unblocked preparation were a separate increase. Dopamine therefore acts on the membrane directly as well as on firing.

A direct or locally mediated membrane effect is therefore supported. The specific ionic conductance responsible is identified in later pharmacological work, because this control shows that spikes are not required for the depolarization.
30: A **D1-like receptor** is a dopamine receptor class that modulates cell signaling rather than forming the spike-generating sodium pore. Liao and colleagues compared dopamine with the D1-like agonist SKF-38393 in adult male zebra finch RA projection neurons.

The agonist increased excitability, and the D1-like antagonist SCH-23390 prevented the dopamine-associated increase under the study's conditions. Comparing an agonist with a receptor blocker gives converging pharmacological evidence for the receptor class involved.

The D1-like effect on RA membrane physiology was measured directly. Area X has a different circuit organization, so the receptor effect there is a separate result. Dopamine receptors of the D1-like class modulate signaling, which changes excitability in these neurons, and the receptor subtype and downstream enzyme are identified by separate work.
31: **D2-like receptors** form a dopamine receptor class that is pharmacologically distinct from D1-like receptors. Liao and colleagues applied the D2-like agonist quinpirole to RA projection neurons and compared firing and membrane voltage before, during and after application.

Quinpirole did not reproduce the strong increase in excitability that dopamine and the D1-like agonist produced in this preparation. The D2-like response is therefore judged against the D1-like response. Receptor class decides the outcome in these neurons.

A weak or absent effect under these conditions leaves D2-like function open in other parts of the song system. Receptor expression and release patterns in those regions are measured separately. The D2-like result therefore applies to this cell population and this preparation.
32: **LMAN**, the lateral magnocellular nucleus of the anterior nidopallium, is a forebrain output of the anterior forebrain pathway. Garst-Orozco and colleagues stimulated HVC and LMAN fiber tracts separately while recording excitatory postsynaptic currents in RA projection neurons.

An **excitatory postsynaptic current** is the membrane current produced when excitatory transmitter activates receptors on the recorded cell. Pathway-specific stimulation let the strength and receptor contributions of the two convergent inputs be compared in juvenile and adult zebra finches.

RA receives input from a direct motor-related pathway and from a basal ganglia–thalamic pathway. The slice stimulation activates the fibers that survive the preparation, and the natural activity of these inputs during a particular syllable is measured in the intact bird.
33: Garst-Orozco and colleagues measured HVC-to-RA currents with weak stimulation, which produced either failures or a consistent single-fiber response. They also used stronger stimulation that recruited the available input population.

Median single-fiber HVC currents rose from about 23 pA in subsong birds to 60 pA in adults. The estimated number of inputs first increased and then declined during later development. The experiment therefore identifies refinement rather than a uniform strengthening.

Strengthening and pruning change how RA converts HVC activity into motor output. The measurements show which inputs are kept and how their number changes through development. Median single-fiber currents rose from about 23 pA in subsong birds to 60 pA in adults, so each kept input drives RA more strongly.
34: Garst-Orozco and colleagues applied the same single-fiber and maximal-recruitment strategy to the LMAN input onto RA neurons. Recordings from subsong, plastic-song and adult birds tested whether the increase in song stereotypy reflected a simple loss of this excitatory pathway.

Mean single-fiber LMAN currents were about 146 pA in plastic-song birds and 142 pA in adults, and the estimated number of available inputs stayed relatively stable. The finding contrasted with the strengthening and pruning of HVC inputs measured in the same framework.

Reduced behavioral variability therefore coexists with persistent LMAN-to-RA connectivity. A preserved connection can have a different influence when other convergent inputs and network activity change, so the same connection supports different roles at different ages.
35: Garst-Orozco and colleagues recorded LMAN-evoked currents at −70 and +40 mV. At negative voltages, extracellular magnesium blocks the **NMDA receptor** current. Depolarization relieves this block, which allows the slower receptor component to contribute.

At −70 mV the response is mostly AMPA-mediated, while at +40 mV the combined AMPA and NMDA response is measured. The estimated NMDA-to-AMPA contribution in subsong birds was about 9:1, so NMDA receptors dominate the LMAN response. Depolarization relieves the magnesium block that suppresses NMDA current at negative voltages.

Voltage-dependent gating means the effect of LMAN input depends partly on the postsynaptic state of RA. The receptor contributions are measured under these voltage conditions, and their role during singing follows from the same gating.
36: Garst-Orozco and colleagues measured RA responses to 0.5-second current pulses at 35 °C across subsong, plastic-song and adult stages. Input-to-firing gain and spike-frequency adaptation were broadly similar across these groups, which constrains a simple intrinsic-excitability explanation of reduced song variability.

Zemel and colleagues included younger 20-day birds and isolated sodium-current components, and they found pronounced maturation of resurgent current and spike properties. The two studies differ in developmental window, recording conditions and the property measured.

A stable firing-rate response over one age interval fits with earlier maturation of a particular ion current. The two results together show that RA intrinsic properties change in some respects and remain stable in others. The developmental account therefore depends on which property is measured at which age.
37: Bottjer and colleagues lesioned the region then called MAN in male zebra finches at different stages of song development. Postoperative vocalizations were recorded repeatedly, and histology sorted complete lesions from partial ones. The timing of each lesion defines the developmental stage at which the bird was operated.

Lesions made early in development produced abnormal vocal patterns, whereas adult birds with complete bilateral lesions kept normal song for as long as five weeks. Birds operated at intermediate stages differed according to how established their song was at the time of the lesion.

Early lesions disrupt the development of vocal behavior, whereas adult lesions leave established song largely intact. LMAN therefore has different functions at different stages of life. Bottjer and colleagues lesioned at several developmental stages in the same male zebra finches, so the same nucleus contributes to developing song and to maintaining adult song at different ages.
38: **Area X** is a song-related basal ganglia region that contains striatal-like neurons and pallidal-like output neurons. These cell classes occupy different positions in the circuit rather than forming one homogeneous population. Striatal-like input and pallidal-like output are the two ends of this processing chain.

Area X receives HVC and LMAN input and sends inhibitory output to the medial portion of the dorsolateral thalamic nucleus, DLM. DLM projects to LMAN, whose output returns to RA and also to Area X, which forms an anatomically connected forebrain loop.

**GABA**, gamma-aminobutyric acid, is the inhibitory transmitter of the pallidal-like output. The pathway constrains the possible mechanisms, and the moment-to-moment activity and learning rule of the loop are measured in the bird's song. The transmitter of the pallidal-like output is therefore central to how Area X shapes its target.
39: A **retrograde tracer** labels neurons that project toward an injection site, whereas an **anterograde tracer** labels their axons and terminals downstream. Vates and Nottebohm used complementary tracing to investigate pathways linking the anterior forebrain with RA.

Injections associated with Area X and RA labeled neurons and terminal fields in LMAN. These distributions support an LMAN output route to both the basal ganglia region and the motor nucleus, which extends the circuit beyond a one-way chain. The pattern matches the projection described for Area X and RA together.

Using more than one tracer direction reduces ambiguity about which cells send and which receive a projection. The tracing identifies the projection, and the function of each route is tested with separate measurements. Two tracer directions therefore give complementary views of the same pathway.
40: Vates and Nottebohm placed different **retrograde tracers** in RA and Area X to ask whether the two projections came from separate LMAN populations. Neurons containing both labels were found within LMAN, which shows output toward both targets from individual cells.

This result is more specific than overlapping terminal fields, because it links the two targets to a shared projecting neuron. A neuron with branching output can influence RA motor circuitry while also returning activity to the anterior forebrain loop through Area X.

Two retrograde tracers placed in RA and Area X label LMAN neurons that project to both sites, so single cells can send collateral branches to both targets. Such dual projections provide one anatomical route for sending related activity to motor and basal ganglia pathways at once.
41: Doupe recorded extracellular spikes from LMAN while playing the bird's own song and comparison sounds to anesthetized adult zebra finches. A raster plot shows the spike times of each neuron across repeated trials, and averaging those trials gives the response profile.

Many neurons responded strongly to the bird's own song and weakly to other conspecific songs or simple acoustic stimuli. Comparisons with amplitude-modulated noise and tones tested whether the response could be explained by a generic sound-evoked response.

The selectivity links an anterior forebrain nucleus with the acoustic structure of learned vocal behavior. These are playback responses recorded under anesthesia, and their role in singing is examined in awake birds. The selectivity and the anesthetic condition are both part of the description of these responses.
42: Doupe compared responses to intact song with altered versions in which the order or arrangement of song elements was changed. A **syllable** is a recognizable acoustic unit, and reorganizing syllables keeps many local features while changing their temporal context.

Some LMAN neurons responded more strongly to the normal sequence than to rearrangements or isolated combinations. These comparisons test whether selectivity depends on one sound fragment alone or on the relation between fragments across time.

Sensitivity to temporal order fits integration of a learned sequence rather than detection of a single frequency. The selectivity mechanism at the synapse is identified by separate experiments, and the roles of recognition, prediction and vocal learning are tested in awake birds.
43: Doupe recorded auditory responses in Area X using the bird's own song, reversed song and songs from other zebra finches. Comparing several stimuli within the same neuron controlled for differences in overall excitability between cells.

Area X neurons responded selectively to familiar self-song, and the responses depended on the temporal structure of the playback. Auditory selectivity is therefore present in the basal ganglia portion of the anterior forebrain pathway. Responses were recorded to the bird's own song and to altered versions of it.

These findings establish sensory responsiveness in a song-related circuit. Area X is characterized here as a sensory-responsive region, and its storage role is tested with separate measurements. The sensory responses are therefore part of the circuit's processing before any motor function is assigned.
44: Gale and Perkel recorded neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta and the ventral tegmental area, SNc/VTA, while testing auditory responses. These midbrain regions provide dopaminergic input to Area X, and the transmitter of each recorded neuron is identified with a separate label.

They combined spike measurements with juxtacellular labeling and immunostaining for **tyrosine hydroxylase**, an enzyme involved in catecholamine synthesis. Labeled cells with the marker gave an anatomical and biochemical check on the classification based on firing properties.

The fluorescent micrographs keep 20 µm scale bars and connect each recorded cell with its tissue identity. Marker-positive cells support the dopaminergic interpretation in this preparation, and the histological identification of each recorded neuron is more specific than a waveform criterion.
45: **Disinhibition** is increased activity that follows the reduction of inhibitory input. Gale and Perkel found that song playback excited Area X neurons, inhibited neurons in the ventral pallidum and excited identified dopaminergic SNc/VTA neurons.

Activating Area X with glutamate increased downstream dopaminergic firing, whereas GABA injection reduced it. Blocking AMPA and NMDA receptors in Area X diminished song-evoked dopaminergic responses, and vehicle injections served as the control.

The convergent recordings and interventions support a route through which song-related forebrain activity regulates its own dopamine supply. The route is consistent with the anatomy in the preceding slides, and its behavioral role is measured separately.
